extracted.intended_audience: DHS officials, immigration attorneys, advocates, and the regulated public (applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and evaluative criteria for determining whether a noncitizen is inadmissible as a 'public charge' under INA sec. 212(a)(4), including what evidence officers should consider and how factors should be weighed in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'likely at any time to become a public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes removing the 2022 Final Rule definition (which equated the phrase to primary dependence on government for subsistence demonstrated by receipt of public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization) and moving away from bright-line primary dependence standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would allow officers to evaluate likelihood to become a public charge consistent with the statute and congressional intent — focusing on whether an alien relies on public resources to meet needs and whether they can rely on own capabilities, family, sponsors, or private organizations. The determination should be case-by-case and fact-specific rather than based on a narrow regulatory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of any means-tested public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to remove regulatory limits that confined consideration to only public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization, allowing receipt of any means-tested public benefit to be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers would consider current and/or past receipt of any means-tested public benefit (e.g., SNAP, CHIP, Medicaid, housing benefits), treating such receipt as one factor among many in the totality of the circumstances. DHS notes that some non-cash benefits may have aggregate costs similar to cash assistance and are relevant to self-sufficiency assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires consideration of the alien's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although DHS proposes removing regulatory repetition of these factors, officers will continue to collect and consider information pertinent to these categories (household size, income, assets, liabilities, education, skills, and receipt of means-tested benefits) in the totality of the circumstances assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances test
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations must be made on a case-by-case basis considering the totality of the alien's circumstances; no single factor (other than lack of a required sufficient Affidavit of Support) should automatically control the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers should weigh all relevant evidence together. Past precedent and federal courts endorse this approach. Receipt of benefits, disability, or any single item should not be dispositive without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (Section 213A) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient Affidavit of Support is a statutory instrument but the statute permits, but does not require, DHS to consider it favorably; DHS proposes removing a regulatory mandate to favorably consider a sufficient affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers will exercise discretion whether and how to consider an affidavit of support in the totality of circumstances. A sufficient affidavit does not automatically establish that an alien is not likely to become a public charge; it is not a guarantee but a contract to permit reimbursement by sponsoring agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on disability
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not treat an alien's disability alone as outcome-determinative in a public charge inadmissibility determination, consistent with section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers may consider disabilities insofar as they affect ability to be self-sufficient, but disability must not be the sole basis for a finding of likely to become a public charge. This mirrors existing legal prohibitions against discrimination based solely on disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of nature, recency, duration, amount, and reason for benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating receipt of public benefits, officers should examine the nature of the benefit, whether it meets basic needs, recency, duration and amount of receipt, reason for receipt, and whether that reason is likely to persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An officer would not find inadmissibility solely because an alien received a means-tested benefit; rather the surrounding circumstances of benefit receipt determine its weight in the totality analysis. For institutionalization, consider whether institutionalization violates federal law (e.g., ADA) if relevant evidence is submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applications/approvals/certifications to receive benefits in future
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider evidence that an alien is trying to receive and/or has been approved or certified to receive means-tested public benefits in the future as relevant to likelihood of becoming dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospective benefit eligibility or approved certifications may indicate a higher likelihood of future dependence and thus are relevant evidence in forward-looking determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of benefits received while in exempt immigration categories
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes removing regulatory provisions that excluded consideration of benefits received while an alien was in a category exempt from the public charge ground; past receipt while exempt may be considered if the alien now seeks a non-exempt benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of means-tested benefits while in an exempt status (e.g., refugees, certain humanitarian categories) can be relevant when the alien later applies for an immigration benefit subject to the public charge ground; officers should account for time-limited eligibility and other circumstances when weighing such receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line time frame or numeric threshold for benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS rejects limiting the public charge assessment to receiving one or more benefits for specific month counts (e.g., 12 months in 36) or to primary dependence standards; statute and precedent do not prescribe a specific degree of receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than fixed numerical thresholds, officers should use a nuanced, interpretive approach informed by precedent to evaluate whether an alien is incapable of earning a livelihood, lacks sufficient funds or support, and in fact receives public support as part of the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of narrow regulatory definitions (receipt, public cash assistance, long-term institutionalization, government, household)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to eliminate several 2022 Final Rule definitions (e.g., receipt, public cash assistance for income maintenance, long-term institutionalization, government, household) that unduly limited evidence considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes ordinary meanings of these terms and statutory guidance suffice for officers to conduct individualized determinations while DHS develops policy and interpretive tools. Removing these definitions expands the universe of evidence officers may consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of past precedent and circuit case law to guide determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a finalized new regulatory definition, DHS intends to make determinations consistent with mandatory statutory factors, relevant circuit precedent, and established precedent decisions that historically informed public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past decisions favor a nuanced, individualized approach. Officers should follow governing precedent and case law to ensure determinations are lawful and consistent with congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of one or more means-tested benefits treated as one factor among many
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an alien received one or more means-tested public benefits, that fact is not automatically dispositive and should be treated as one of many considerations in the totality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers must examine accompanying circumstances (why benefits were received, ability to be self-supporting, family/sponsor support) rather than assuming benefit receipt equals inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain denials in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS officers are required under 8 CFR 103.3(a)(1)(i) to explain in writing the specific reasons for a denial of an application, including denials based on public charge inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although DHS proposes not to restate a regulatory provision mandating written explanations specific to public charge determinations, officers will continue to issue written denials that specify the factors and basis for the decision per existing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection and discretionary requests for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will continue to collect information relevant to statutory minimum factors (e.g., Form I-693 medical exam, Form I-485, interviews) and may request additional evidence on a case-by-case basis as indicated by the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers should request supplementary documentation when necessary to clarify circumstances bearing on age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education and skills, and benefit receipt. The format of data collection may be adjusted for practical utility but the substantive information remains collected.
